claims.text: Under conventional ambient-pressure quenching, Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 rapidly forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence during cooling and reheating.
Applying a hydrostatic pressure of approximately 1–2 GPa during melt quenching will increase amorphous retention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Applying high pressure during melt quenching will improve the thermal stability of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
High-pressure melt quenching will suppress nucleation of primary crystalline phases.
High-pressure melt quenching will suppress growth of primary crystalline phases.
High pressure increases the effective viscosity of the alloy melt.
High pressure alters the free-energy landscape such that the thermodynamic driving force for nucleation of primary phases is reduced.
High pressure reduces atomic mobility during solidification.
High pressure increases the kinetic barrier for crystal nucleation.
Reduced atomic mobility and an increased nucleation barrier favor retention of an amorphous or metastably supercooled structure.
High-pressure-quenched samples will have a higher amorphous phase fraction than ambient-pressure-quenched samples.
High-pressure-quenched samples will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature during reheating than ambient-pressure-quenched samples.
High-pressure-quenched samples will show lower-intensity DSC crystallization exotherms than ambient-pressure-quenched samples.
High-pressure-quenched samples will show fewer DSC crystallization exotherms than ambient-pressure-quenched samples.
The intervention is anticipated to be effective from approximately 1 to 2 GPa.
The intervention is anticipated to be effective at cooling rates from approximately 10^3 to 10^5 K/s.
Outside the proposed pressure and cooling-rate bounds, pressure may be insufficient to delay nucleation or may induce unwanted phase transformations.
Prior data on high-pressure quenching specifically for Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 are limited.

contradictions.description: The conditions define rapid cooling as greater than 10^5 K/s, whereas the stated effective boundary ends at approximately 10^5 K/s. Thus, part of the proposed rapid-cooling experiment lies outside the claimed effective range.
